section.title: Judgment Against Samaria and Judah
section.sectionRationale: The book opens like a courtroom summons to the whole earth. The LORD Himself descends from His temple to tread the high places, and the reason is named plainly: the sin of His own people, embodied in their two capitals, Samaria and Jerusalem. The chapter moves from a cosmic theophany to a very local lament, as Micah walks weeping through the towns of his own Judean homeland toward the coming Assyrian storm.
section.thesis: The God who dwells in heaven comes down to judge, because the sin of His covenant people has infected both kingdoms from the capitals outward; yet the prophet who announces the ruin weeps over it, and the judgment is aimed at idolatry, not at the destruction of hope.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the LORD comes down as witness and judge against His people (1-5); the sentence on Samaria the idol city (6-7); and Micah's barefoot lament as calamity rolls through the towns of Judah to the gate of Jerusalem (8-16).

units.label: The LORD comes down to judge
units.note: a summons to all the earth

verses.text: This is the word of the LORD that came to {{micah|Micah}} the Moreshite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, what he saw regarding Samaria and Jerusalem:
Hear, O peoples, all of you; listen, O earth, and everyone in it! May the Lord GOD bear witness against you, the Lord from His holy temple.
For behold, the LORD comes forth from His dwelling place; He will come down and tread on the high places of the earth.
The mountains will melt beneath Him, and the valleys will split apart, like wax before the fire, like water rushing down a slope.

All this is for the {{pesha|transgression}} of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?
Therefore I will make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard. I will pour her stones into the valley and expose her foundations.

All her carved images will be smashed to pieces; all her wages will be burned in the fire, and I will destroy all her idols. Since she collected the wages of a prostitute, they will be used again on a prostitute.

units.label: The prophet's lament through the towns

verses.text: Because of this I will lament and wail; I will walk barefoot and naked. I will howl like a jackal and mourn like an ostrich.
For her wound is incurable; it has reached even Judah; it has approached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem itself.
Do not tell it in Gath; do not weep at all. Roll in the dust in Beth-leaphrah.
Depart in shameful nakedness, O dwellers of Shaphir. The dwellers of Zaanan will not come out. Beth-ezel is in mourning; its support is taken from you.
For the dwellers of Maroth pined for good, but calamity came down from the LORD, even to the gate of Jerusalem.
Harness your chariot horses, O dweller of Lachish. You were the beginning of sin to the Daughter of Zion, for the transgressions of Israel were found in you.
Therefore, send farewell gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib will prove deceptive to the kings of Israel.
I will again bring a conqueror against you, O dweller of Mareshah. The glory of Israel will come to Adullam.
Shave yourselves bald and cut off your hair in mourning for your precious children; make yourselves as bald as an eagle, for they will go from you into exile.

micah.gloss: The prophet's name is a shortened form of a question, Who is like the LORD? It is a small sermon in a single word. The book that opens with this name closes in 7:18 by answering it: Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity? The judgment announced here and the mercy promised there both flow from the incomparable God whose name Micah carries.

pesha.gloss: Transgression, rebellion, a willful breach of relationship. It is stronger than a simple mistake; it pictures a deliberate revolt against a rightful lord. Micah traces the coming ruin not to bad luck or mere weakness but to the covenant people's rebellion, which had settled into their very capitals, Samaria and Jerusalem.

basic.context: Micah was a country preacher from Moresheth, a small town in the Judean lowlands, who spoke for God in the same years as Isaiah, roughly 750 to 700 years before Christ. He watched the northern kingdom, with its capital Samaria, fall to Assyria, and he warned that the same judgment was rolling south toward Jerusalem. Chapter one opens like a courtroom: God summons the whole earth, comes down from heaven, and names the charge, the sin of His own people.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real prophecy about real cities, and much of it came true within Micah's lifetime when Assyria devastated the land. The point is not that God is cruel but that sin, especially idolatry, is deadly serious even, and especially, among God's own people. The many town names in verses 10 to 16 are a series of grief-stricken puns, Micah weeping his way through his own neighborhood as the disaster approaches.
basic.originalLanguages: The prophet's very name, Micah, is short for the question Who is like the LORD? The charge against the people is pesha, transgression, a word for deliberate rebellion, not a mere slip. So the God who is beyond compare is met not with worship but with revolt, and that revolt had taken up residence in the two capital cities.
basic.typology: The LORD coming down to tread the high places foreshadows every coming of God in judgment, and ultimately the day when Christ returns to judge the earth. The prophet who weeps over the doomed cities anticipates Jesus weeping over Jerusalem, a judge whose heart breaks over those He must warn.
basic.christ: Micah's tears over a guilty people point straight to Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem and said, how often I have longed to gather your children. The God who comes down here to judge is the same God who will come down in the flesh to save. And the incurable wound of verse 9 finds its only cure at the cross, where the judgment falls on Christ instead of us.
basic.god: God is holy and cannot ignore sin, even in the people He loves. He is also the true King who sees, who summons, who acts, and who is grieved. He is not indifferent to idolatry; He treats it as spiritual adultery. Yet even His judgment has a purpose: to strip away the idols that were destroying His people.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 17 records the fall of Samaria that Micah foresaw. Jeremiah 26 remembers how Micah's preaching moved King Hezekiah to repentance. Luke 19 shows Jesus weeping over Jerusalem as Micah wept over Judah. Amos 4 pictures the same God treading the high places of the earth.
basic.oneStory: The book of Micah begins where the whole Bible often begins, with a holy God confronting the sin of His people. But the tears of the prophet already hint that judgment is not the last word. The God who is like no other, whose name Micah carries, will make a way to pardon the very rebellion He here condemns, a way that runs through Bethlehem and the cross.

context.literary:
The book opens with a title in verse 1 that is already a statement of method. It calls what follows 'the word of the LORD' and then says it is 'what he saw regarding Samaria and Jerusalem.' The verb is the ordinary one for seeing, so Micah receives a word that he also perceives, a message with pictures in it. The two capitals named at the head of the book are the two subjects of everything after, and the chapter will not let them stand apart: Samaria in verses 6 and 7, Jerusalem in verses 9 and 12.

The chapter moves in three steps that grow smaller and nearer. Verses 2 to 4 are cosmic. A summons goes to all peoples and to the earth, the Lord comes out of His temple, and the mountains melt. Verses 5 to 7 name the cause and carry out the sentence on Samaria. Verses 8 to 16 then come to ground in Micah's own countryside. The camera starts at the throne of heaven and ends in a dozen small villages. The nearer it comes, the more personal the speech becomes, until the prophet is howling and barefoot.

The cosmic opening has the shape of a courtroom. 'Hear' in verse 2 is the opening call of a lawsuit, and the Lord is called to 'bear witness against you.' The same call returns in Micah 6:1-2, where the Lord has 'a case against His people.' The two summonses bracket the first six chapters of the book. The call also echoes Deuteronomy 32:1, where Moses calls heaven and earth to witness the covenant.

A fine piece of design sits in verses 3 and 5. The Lord treads on the 'high places of the earth,' and Micah then asks what Judah's 'high place' is, and answers that it is Jerusalem. The same word, high place, names both the mountains under God's feet and the shrines of false worship, so that the capital which should have been the place of the Lord's presence is named as a rival shrine. Verses 10 to 16 then turn to a long run of wordplays. The BSB footnotes record the sounds: Gath sounds like 'tell,' Beth-leaphrah means 'house of dust,' Maroth sounds like 'bitter,' Achzib means 'deception.' The poetry makes the geography speak, and the sound of each name carries the doom of the town.
context.historical:
Micah prophesied in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, verse 1, which spans the second half of the eighth century before Christ. His oracle on Samaria in verses 6 and 7 stands before its fall, which came after a siege of three years, 2 Kings 17:5, and the exile of the northern tribes to Assyria, 2 Kings 17:6. Samaria had been founded by Omri, who bought the hill from Shemer, 1 Kings 16:24, and by Micah's day it was the proud capital of the northern kingdom and a centre of the worship of other gods, so its conversion into a vineyard slope was a vivid reversal.

Micah's own home, Moresheth, lay in the Shephelah, the low hills between the Judean highlands and the coastal plain, on the road the Assyrians would take. Many of the towns in verses 10 to 15 lie in that region. Lachish and Mareshah were among the cities that Rehoboam fortified, 2 Chronicles 11:5-9, which shows how vulnerable the Judean heartland was and why these were the front line. In 701 BC Sennacherib attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah, 2 Kings 18:13, and Hezekiah sent his submission to him while the king was at Lachish, 2 Kings 18:14. Sennacherib's own palace at Nineveh was later decorated with a long relief of his siege of Lachish. The oracle in Micah 1 is therefore not about a distant event. It describes the terrain Micah knew and the roads his neighbours would be driven along.

The idolatry condemned in verse 7 was both religious and economic. The 'wages of a prostitute' recall the gifts brought to the shrines of the fertility gods, and Hosea, Micah's contemporary in the north, describes Israel as playing the harlot and making 'love for hire on every threshing floor,' Hosea 9:1. Deuteronomy 23:18 forbade bringing such wages into the house of the Lord. Micah's charge is that the capitals have turned worship into a trade and filled the temple treasuries with it.

Verse 9 says the wound reaches Judah, 'the gate of my people.' The gate was the place of justice and assembly, so the threat is not only military but civil and religious. The sign-acts of verse 8 also have precedent: Isaiah, working in Jerusalem at the same period, walked naked and barefoot as a sign, Isaiah 20:2. Public mourning, shaved heads and rolling in dust, verses 10 and 16, were the accepted ways of grieving and are mentioned elsewhere in the prophets as the response to national disaster.
context.canonical:
The picture of the Lord coming out of His dwelling is one of the oldest in the Old Testament, and Micah assumes his hearers know it. At Sinai the mountains quaked before the LORD, Judges 5:4-5. The psalmist sings that 'the mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD,' Psalm 97:5. Nahum and Habakkuk use the same imagery, Nahum 1:5 and Habakkuk 3:6, and Isaiah says 'the LORD is coming out of His dwelling to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity,' Isaiah 26:21. Amos had described the same Lord who 'strides on the heights of the earth,' Amos 4:13. What is new in Micah is the direction. In Judges and the Psalms the Lord comes down to rescue His people from their enemies. Here He comes against His people.

Micah's courtroom language links the chapter to the covenant. When Moses called heaven and earth to witness the covenant, Deuteronomy 32:1, he warned of this very day. The opening of Micah is the covenant lawsuit being served.

The memory of Micah's preaching was kept. A century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for prophesying against the temple, some elders stood up and cited Micah of Moresheth, who in Hezekiah's reign had said that Zion would be plowed like a field, Jeremiah 26:18, which is Micah 3:12. They remembered that Hezekiah did not kill him but sought the Lord, and that the Lord relented, Jeremiah 26:19. The elders thus show that Micah's judgments were conditional in practice: his warnings produced repentance, and repentance produced mercy.

In the New Testament the same pattern returns. Peter writes that judgment begins with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17, as Micah began with Samaria and Jerusalem. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as He draws near, Luke 19:41, and foretells that not one stone will be left on another because the city did not recognize the time of its visitation, Luke 19:44. The Lord's coming 'from heaven in blazing fire,' 2 Thessalonians 1:7, and the mountains moved from their place in Revelation 6:14 take Micah's opening to its final fulfilment, the day when the great and small hide from the face of the One seated on the throne.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Micah wanted his hearers to understand, first, that the God they thought of as present in the temple and on their side was the one who was about to come out against them. The opening verses are built to unsettle. The call goes out to all peoples and the whole earth, as though the case against Judah were so public that creation itself must hear it. Then he narrows it to the two capitals. The thing that concerns the Lord is not the sin of foreigners but the sin of Jacob and the house of Israel, and its centre is in the places that should have been the nation's pride.

He also wanted his hearers to see where corruption begins. The question 'What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria?' makes the capital the source of the national disease, and the answer about Jerusalem makes the same claim of the southern kingdom. The people were looking to their leaders and sanctuaries as their security, and Micah says these are the problem. This was a hard thing to say in Jerusalem, and later generations remembered that Micah dared to say it.

Finally he wanted them to hear grief in the verdict. The prophet does not stand over the ruin. He howls like a jackal and goes barefoot, and the detailed lament over the towns of verses 10 to 16 shows a man who loves the places he names. He is not neutral and he is not triumphant. He announces the judgment as one who belongs to the people who will suffer it, 'the gate of my people,' and in that way he teaches that the right response to the word of judgment is lament and repentance, not complacency. Hezekiah's later response, recalled in Jeremiah 26:19, suggests that Micah was heard.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a historical judgment on two capitals, announced for specific sins and carried out by Assyria. It does not tell believers to wish destruction on anyone, nor does it say that every disaster is God's judgment on a particular people. The text itself ties this disaster to a named charge, idolatry and rebellion in the covenant people, and to a word of the Lord given before the event. Without such a word, readers should be careful about reading calamities as messages.

The lament is described as the prophet's practice. His barefoot walk, his howling and the shaved heads of verse 16 were suited to his time and place, and nobody today is bound to copy the outward form. What carries over is the inward posture: the preacher who announces God's judgment should do it with tears, not triumph, and the community that hears should mourn what the sin has cost.

Another thing the passage describes, but does not recommend, is the way false worship had been made profitable, 'the wages of a prostitute.' The point is not that wealth is evil but that religion bought and sold, or shaped to bring in money, is an offence to the Lord. The New Testament carries the same concern, and 1 Peter 4:17 reminds the church that scrutiny begins with God's own household. A church that reads Micah 1 is meant to ask what its own high places are.

debates.question: Are the coming of the LORD and the melting mountains in verses 3 to 4 literal or figurative?

views.label: Poetic theophany language
views.case: The imagery draws on the standard vocabulary of God appearing at Sinai and in the Psalms, Judges 5:4-5 and Psalm 97:5. Melting mountains and splitting valleys are vivid poetry for the overwhelming approach of the Judge, not a geological forecast.

views.label: Real historical intervention
views.case: The poetry describes an actual coming of God in the historical judgments of Assyria against Samaria and Judah, and points forward to the final day when God truly shakes the earth, as in Revelation 6:14.

debates.bearing: Either way the point is the same: the living God really acts in history to judge sin, and no created power can stand before Him when He comes. The language is true to what happened, whether or not the mountains moved.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verse 8, and who is howling like a jackal?

views.label: Micah the prophet
views.case: The speaker is the one who calls the gate 'the gate of my people' in verse 9 and who walks through his own home towns in the verses that follow. Prophets acted out their messages, as Isaiah did in Isaiah 20:2, and Micah's grief is a sign-act that makes the loss visible before it happens.

views.label: The LORD Himself
views.case: Verses 6 and 7 are in the voice of God, 'I will make Samaria a heap of rubble' and 'I will destroy all her idols,' and verse 8 begins 'Because of this I will lament,' with no change of speaker marked. On this reading God mourns the judgment He brings, a reading that fits Hosea 11:8, where His heart is turned within Him.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew leaves the speaker open, and the two readings do not conflict. The prophet's tears are the Lord's tears given a human voice, and the book shows a God who judges with grief. The reader should not choose so sharply that either is lost.

study.originalLanguages:
The title in verse 1 says that Micah 'saw' the word. The verb chazah is the ordinary word for a prophet's vision and gives the prophets one of their titles, 'seer.' Micah's message is given to him as something perceived, and the chapter that follows is full of things seen: the mountains melting, the heap of rubble in a field, the barefoot prophet, the towns in a line. The word of the LORD comes as picture and sound together.

The Hebrew word for 'witness' in verse 2 is ed, the same word used of a witness in a legal case, so the Lord is called to 'bear witness against you.' The prophet is not simply a messenger but a witness in the covenant lawsuit that Micah 6:1-2 will describe. The verb shama, 'hear,' that opens verse 2 is the covenant summons, as in the Shema, and the call goes out to 'all of you,' peoples and earth alike.

The word for 'high places' in verse 3 and 'high place' in verse 5 is bamah. In the first place it names the heights of the earth under the Lord's feet, and in the second it names the sites of unauthorised worship that the law had ordered destroyed, Deuteronomy 12:2-3. By using one word for both, Micah makes the Lord's tread on the heights an answer to the people's tread on their own altars. The location of the Lord's authority, over every height, is what the shrines have forgotten.

In verse 7 the 'wages of a prostitute' is etnan zonah. The same expression appears in the law forbidding such wages to be brought into the house of the Lord, Deuteronomy 23:18, and Hosea uses the same word in the phrase 'love for hire,' Hosea 9:1. The sentence says that what was collected from false worship will go back into the same economy. The enemy will carry off the idols' treasure and spend it on its own temples.

The wound of verse 9 is called incurable, anush. The same word describes Jeremiah's pain, 'my wound incurable, refusing to be healed,' Jeremiah 15:18, and the Lord's verdict on Judah, 'Your injury is incurable; your wound is grievous,' Jeremiah 30:12. The word suggests a sickness beyond any human remedy. Isaiah, his contemporary, describes the nation as a body wounded from the sole of the foot to the head, Isaiah 1:5-6.

The long run of town names in verses 10 to 15 depends on sound. The BSB footnotes list the key cases. The prophet tells Gath not to 'tell' it, and the name Gath sounds like the Hebrew word for 'tell.' This echoes David's lament, 'Tell it not in Gath,' 2 Samuel 1:20, so a famous line of national mourning is turned into a line of mourning for Judah. Beth-leaphrah means 'house of dust,' so its people are told to roll in dust. Zaanan sounds like 'come out,' and its people will not come out. Maroth sounds like 'bitter,' Lachish like 'team of horses,' Moresheth like 'gift,' or 'dowry,' Achzib means 'deception,' and Mareshah sounds like 'conqueror.' The prophet speaks in puns because the towns are about to become what their names say.

Verse 16 tells the people to make themselves 'as bald as an eagle.' The Hebrew bird may refer to the eagle or to a vulture, and the picture of a bald head is the point. Shaving the head was a mark of grief, and the children, called 'precious,' are the ones being lost to exile.

typology.type: The wound that cannot be healed, Micah 1:9
typology.fulfillment: Micah describes a sickness that has spread from Samaria to the gate of Jerusalem and has no human cure. Isaiah's picture of a body wounded from head to foot, Isaiah 1:5-6, fills it out. The New Testament says the healing came through a wound: Christ 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' and 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24. The escalation is that the incurable wound is borne by another. The type falls short in that Micah's wound is judgment on a nation, while the healing is given to individuals and the church.

typology.type: The LORD coming down to the high places, Micah 1:3
typology.fulfillment: The Lord leaves His dwelling and comes down to the earth. The pattern reaches its centre in the incarnation, when 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. Micah's coming is one of judgment, and Jesus Himself will return 'from heaven in blazing fire,' 2 Thessalonians 1:7, when the mountains are moved from their place, Revelation 6:14. The first coming was in humility to save; the final coming is the day Micah's theophany points to. The type is incomplete until both comings are seen together.

Micah goes barefoot and howls over a city he must warn. This anticipates the Lord who 'saw the city, He wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and who longed to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks, Matthew 23:37. The prophet's tears are the best that a man can offer. In Jesus the weeping comes from the one who has the power to judge and the power to save, and who will carry the judgment Himself. Micah weeps over what he cannot prevent; Christ weeps and then goes to the cross.

typology.type: The glory of Israel at Adullam, Micah 1:15
typology.fulfillment: The glory of Israel, taken to mean its nobility, is brought down to a cave at Adullam, the place where David hid and where the distressed gathered around him, 1 Samuel 22:1-2. The text says the glory of Israel will be reduced to a hiding place. The pattern of a humbled royal line fits what Micah 5:2 goes on to promise, a ruler from small Bethlehem. This is a pattern, not a prediction, and it should not be pressed. It shows that the Lord's way of raising a king passes through lowly places, a pattern that Christ fulfils most fully, being born in Bethlehem and gathering the weary, Matthew 11:28.

study.christ:
Micah 1 leads to Christ first by the coming of God. The prophet announces that the LORD 'will come down,' verse 3, and the whole shape of the Bible's story is that He does. The Word who 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, is the Lord come out of His place. Micah sees that coming as judgment, because the people have made themselves enemies of the One who comes. The New Testament holds both: Jesus is the Lord's visitation of mercy, and for those who do not recognize it, a visitation of judgment, as He says over Jerusalem, 'you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God,' Luke 19:44. The chapter's question is whether the people will know the Lord when He appears.

It leads to Christ by the prophet's tears. Micah does not rejoice at the coming ruin. He sits in dust and howls for the towns of his own country. Jesus, approaching the same Jerusalem, weeps, Luke 19:41, and says, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!' Matthew 23:37. The hearts of the two men are alike, but Jesus is not only a prophet who announces the wrath. He is the Lord who comes, and He is the one who takes the wound. The wound of Micah 1:9 is described as incurable, and Peter says of Christ, 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24. The sickness that reaches the gate of Jerusalem is the sickness Christ carries outside the city gate, Hebrews 13:12.

It leads to Christ by the problem of the high places. Micah says that Jerusalem, the city that should have been the place of the Lord's presence, has become a rival shrine. The city that God chose had turned into the city that needed judgment. The answer is a temple not made of stones. Jesus speaks of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, and in Him God's presence is no longer tied to a hill that can be corrupted. The new Jerusalem has no temple, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22.

It leads to Christ by the shape of judgment. Peter's remark that judgment begins with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17, echoes Micah's arrangement, and Peter follows it with the question, 'what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?' The cross is the place where judgment on God's own family falls on the one who is both the Lord and the faithful remnant, so that the people of God are not swept away.

A caution: Micah 1 does not predict Jesus the way Micah 5:2 does. No detail of the town list is a code for the gospel. The links here rest on the New Testament's own use of these themes, the coming of the Lord, the weeping at Jerusalem, the healing of a wound, the new temple. Micah 1 shows the problem, a holy God and a rebellious people, and the rest of the Bible shows how He solves it.
study.god:
The chapter begins with God as witness and judge, and this is a God who speaks with authority over every people. The summons in verse 2 goes to all peoples and the whole earth, so that the case against Judah is heard by the world. The God of Israel is not a local deity who looks after His own people's interests; He is the Lord of heaven who is able to bring Assyria against His people and still hold Assyria accountable. Verse 12 makes this plain, saying that 'calamity came down from the LORD,' even to the gate of Jerusalem. The Assyrian armies are the means and not the cause.

He is transcendent and near. He speaks 'from His holy temple,' which in the book's own terms is His heavenly dwelling, and He treads on the high places of the earth. Psalm 11:4 pictures the Lord in His holy temple on His heavenly throne, His eyes watching the sons of men, and Micah's God is the same. He is far above, and He is not distant. He comes. The mountains give way under Him, which shows the scale of His power, yet the same chapter shows Him dealing with villages like Maroth and Mareshah. Nothing is too large or too small for His attention.

He is holy, and His holiness is not abstract. The two capitals have turned worship into profit and made idols out of the Lord's gifts, and the Lord treats this as unfaithfulness in a marriage. The language of prostitution and wages is the language of broken love. Isaiah said that the faithful city had become a harlot, Isaiah 1:21. God's judgment is not the outburst of a bad temper but the response of a holy God to betrayal of covenant, and it is aimed at the idols as much as the people. The statement that He will 'destroy all her idols' tells us that He means to remove what has been destroying them.

He is also grieved. The speaker of verse 8 mourns, and whether this is the prophet or the Lord, the book teaches that judgment is not a pleasure to God. Ezekiel puts it in the Lord's own mouth, 'I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked,' Ezekiel 33:11. Hosea shows His heart turning within Him, Hosea 11:8. Micah's God is the same: He judges, and His people are still 'my people.'

He is also faithful to His word. The warning came before the event, and it was carried out in history. The Samaria of verse 6 fell, and Jerusalem was not exempt from the principle even if it was spared in Hezekiah's day. God's patience is not a promise that sin will be overlooked.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to approach the God who comes with reverence and honesty. We are to ask what our own high places are, and to meet His word as Micah did, with grief and repentance, trusting that the God who judges His people is also the God who calls them 'my people.'

crossReferences.note: Moses calls heaven and earth to listen to the song that sets out God's covenant dealings with Israel. Micah's call to the peoples and the earth in verse 2 uses the same covenant lawsuit setting. The prophet is serving a summons that Moses had announced in advance, so that the judgment falls under the terms of the covenant.

The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD. Micah's image in verse 4 is nearly identical. In the psalm it is a reason to rejoice that the Lord reigns, while in Micah the same presence is a danger for a people who have turned away. The same God has opposite effects on those who love Him and on those who reject Him.

The One who forms the mountains and strides on the heights of the earth is named as the LORD, the God of Hosts. Micah 1:3 uses that image of the Lord treading on the high places. Amos prophesied in the north a little earlier, and the two prophets share the conviction that the Creator is the Judge.

The king of Assyria besieged Samaria for three years, captured it, and carried the Israelites away. This is the historical fulfilment of the sentence in Micah 1:6-7. The chapter was written before the event and records the exact kind of ruin Micah announced, a city broken and its people sent east.

The law forbids bringing the wages of a prostitute into the house of the Lord. Micah's phrase in verse 7 uses the same expression, and its target is the traffic in worship. The prophets are not inventing new standards but holding the people to the law they already had.

David's lament over Saul and Jonathan begins with the cry 'Tell it not in Gath.' When Micah says 'Do not tell it in Gath' in verse 10, he borrows the cry of national mourning. The grief of Judah is as great as the grief for a fallen king, and for the same reason: the enemy must not hear of it.

Sennacherib attacked and captured the fortified cities of Judah, and Hezekiah sent word to him at Lachish. Micah's town list in verses 10 to 16 describes the ground over which this campaign passed. The oracle reads as an anticipation of what happened, and Lachish is named in both texts.

The elders of Jeremiah's day remember Micah of Moresheth and his warning that Zion would be plowed like a field. They point out that Hezekiah feared the LORD and the LORD relented. It shows that Micah's word was remembered as a call to repentance, and that it worked.

Isaiah, Micah's contemporary in Jerusalem, describes the nation as wounded from the sole of the foot to the top of the head, with no soundness. This is the same condition as the incurable wound in Micah 1:9. Both prophets use the picture of an illness that has spread through the whole body.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its destruction because it did not recognize the time of its visitation. The passage is like Micah 1 in subject and heart: the Lord is coming, the city will not know Him, and the one who warns is weeping. Micah's tears are completed in the tears of the Lord.

Peter says it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God. This is the New Testament counterpart of Micah's insistence that the transgression of Jacob and the sins of Israel are at the head of the charge. God starts with His own people, and the church is not exempt from the principle.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God dwelling with His creatures in a garden and ends with the dwelling place of God among men. Everything between is the story of how that presence was lost and recovered. Micah 1 belongs to the part of the story in which God's presence in Israel has become a threat to Israel, because they have turned the places of His presence into places of false worship. The Lord who walked in the garden, Genesis 3:8, now walks on the high places of the earth, and the movement is toward them as Judge.

The chapter looks back to Sinai, where the mountain shook, and to the command to destroy the high places of the nations, Deuteronomy 12:2-3. Israel was given the land on condition of covenant loyalty, and Micah's charge is that the nation has done what the nations did. The sentence is exile, which in the shape of Scripture is a return to the condition of Eden's gate, a people driven out of the place of God's presence. The captives' march away from the land echoes the movement of Genesis 3:24, a people sent out from the place of God's presence.

It looks forward to the fall of Jerusalem itself. Micah's hearers heard Samaria's doom and were spared in Hezekiah's day, but the principle remained. In 586 BC the house of the LORD and the houses of Jerusalem were burned, 2 Kings 25:9, and in Jesus' day the same fate was foretold again, Luke 19:44. The Lord came near and was not recognized.

It looks forward to Christ, who is the answer to each of the chapter's problems. He is God's coming down in mercy, John 1:14. He is the temple that cannot be corrupted, John 2:19-21. He carries the incurable wound, 1 Peter 2:24. He weeps and then dies for the city that weeps no tears of its own, Luke 19:41. And He will come again, when the mountains are moved from their place and every false refuge is exposed, Revelation 6:14-16.

In the new creation, the movement of Micah 1 is reversed. The high places are gone, since nothing impure will enter and the idolaters are outside, Revelation 22:15. The throne of the Lord and the Lamb stands in the city with no temple, because God Himself dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The barefoot prophet's grief, the rubble in the field and the exile of children are all answered by the voice from the throne. What Micah mourned as the loss of God's presence becomes, in the end, the joy of God with them as their God.

sermon.why: No focused expository sermon on Micah 1 by a trusted expositor could be verified by web search this session, so none is cited rather than risk misattribution.

quiz.q: Why is the LORD coming down to judge, according to verse 5?

options.text: Because of the transgression of Jacob and the sins of Israel, centered in Samaria and Jerusalem.
options.note: Verse 5 names the people's rebellion, lodged in the two capitals, as the cause.

options.text: Because the surrounding pagan nations had attacked Israel.
options.note: Foreign invasion was the means God later used, but verse 5 names His own people's sin as the reason He comes.

options.text: Because the land had suffered a natural disaster.
options.note: The melting mountains are poetry for God's coming; the cause is sin, not nature.

options.text: Because God is arbitrary and simply wished to destroy.
options.note: The text gives a clear moral cause and shows God's grief; He is not arbitrary.

quiz.q: What does the prophet's name, Micah, mean, and why does it matter here?

options.text: Who is like the LORD, underlining that the incomparable God is met with idolatry and rebellion.
options.note: The name frames the book and is answered in 7:18, Who is a God like You who pardons.

options.text: The LORD saves, pointing to deliverance from Assyria.
options.note: That is the meaning of Joshua or Jesus, not Micah.

options.text: Servant of the LORD, stressing Micah's humble role.
options.note: Micah is a servant, but his name specifically asks who is like the LORD.

options.text: Comfort, signaling the book is only about hope.
options.note: The name is a question about God's incomparability, and the book holds both judgment and hope.

quiz.q: How does Micah respond to the judgment he must announce (verse 8)?

options.text: He laments and wails, walking barefoot, grieving over his people.
options.note: Verse 8 shows the prophet weeping, not gloating, over the coming ruin.

options.text: He rejoices that his enemies will finally be punished.
options.note: Micah grieves; there is no gloating over the doom of his people.

options.text: He stays silent and detached from the message.
options.note: He is anything but detached; he mourns openly and dramatically.

options.text: He demands that God relent immediately.
options.note: He grieves and pleads over the coming ruin, though verse 8 shows open lament rather than an explicit demand that God relent.

quiz.q: What is the point of the many town names in verses 10 to 16?

options.text: They are grief-filled wordplays as Micah weeps through his own homeland toward the coming disaster.
options.note: Each town's name is punned with the ruin that befalls it, a geography of lament.

options.text: They list the towns that escaped the judgment untouched.
options.note: The towns are marked for calamity, not spared; the section is a dirge.

options.text: They simply record boundaries for later land division.
options.note: These are real towns of Micah's homeland, but the passage laments their coming ruin rather than recording land boundaries.

options.text: They name the birthplaces of future kings.
options.note: The section is about coming ruin, not royal genealogy.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: The God who comes down to judge, and the prophet who weeps over the city, are fulfilled in Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem and bore the wound of sin.
options.note: Micah's judging God and weeping prophet both find their answer in Christ.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Christ's birth.
options.note: Micah does point toward Christ's birthplace, though that comes in chapter 5 and no date is given; chapter 1 points to Christ more broadly.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The judging, grieving God of Micah 1 is fully revealed in Jesus.

options.text: It teaches that judgment is the final word with no hope.
options.note: The prophet's tears and his name already point beyond judgment to mercy.

questions: Micah names sin plainly, even in God's own people. Where might you be tolerating an idol or a rebellion that you have stopped calling by its true name?
The prophet wept over the judgment he announced. When you think about God's judgment on sin, does it move you to grief and prayer for others, or to indifference or even satisfaction?
God called the people's idolatry spiritual adultery. What competes with God for your deepest loyalty and affection right now?
The wound is called incurable, yet the whole book moves toward the God who pardons. How does it change your view of a besetting sin to know that only Christ, not self-reform, can heal it?
Micah's name asks, Who is like the LORD? Spend a moment answering that question about God's holiness and His mercy. How does holding both together shape the way you come to Him?

translationNotes.note: Moreshite marks Micah as a man of Moresheth-gath, a town in the Judean lowlands, a rural prophet addressing the capitals of both kingdoms.
The creatures rendered jackal and ostrich are uncertain; the BSB footnote offers serpent or dragon, and literally daughters of an ostrich or owl. The sense is a mournful, eerie howling of grief.

This section is built on Hebrew puns tying each town's name to its fate, as the BSB footnotes show: Gath sounds like tell, Beth-leaphrah means house of dust, Shaphir means pleasant, Zaanan sounds like come out, Maroth like bitter, Lachish like team of horses, Achzib means deception, and Mareshah sounds like conqueror.
